comments.body:
No one is goi g to trade AI games for a masterpiece like GTA anytime soon.

comments.author: YKLKTMA
comments.body: No model will be able to make a commercially relevant GTA-level game, not in a year and not in a hundred years, if only because a solo amateur will never have the expertise or resources required to do it.

replies.author: HaMMeReD
replies.body: It'll still be people using AI, just it's really a solo dev with a $200/mo codex budget vs a team of 1000 w/10k month spend for each of them.

replies.author: YKLKTMA
replies.body: Exactly. For some reason, a lot of beginners don’t seem to understand that if a tool is available to them, it’s also available to large corporations that can hire thousands of professionals, buy practically unlimited amounts of compute, and spend essentially unlimited money on marketing.

replies.author: HaMMeReD
replies.body:
The only caveat is the big companies can adapt AI, but they aren't AI first and they are entrenched and move/change slowly. Layers and layers of management and policy.

That said, it's more than just vibe coding a game, it's about building reliable, ai driven processes from the ground up. That's the indie advantage for now, it's agility and versatility. We have the freedom to use the tool anyways we want without red tape. So we can build ai-first companies that can maybe challenge rockstar in 10-15 years with a much smaller budget. But no indie is making a legit GTA clone with AI anytime. There is artistry in it.

replies.author: YKLKTMA
replies.body:
They were built as profit-first organizations, so they’ll worship Satan himself if it turns out to be profitable.

Indies don’t really have much of an advantage here. At my workplace, for example, we have several dedicated experts whose job is to make AI easier to integrate into every part of our workflow. We already log all our meetings, and afterward you can ask a bot in Slack for a short summary of who agreed on what with whom. And that’s not even mentioning the fact that everyone from programmers to game designers uses AI tools directly in their day-to-day work.

They won’t be able to challenge Rockstar unless they have Rockstar-level budgets. Making games of that scale is extremely difficult and extremely expensive. Even Ubisoft can’t afford to make its own GTA.

comments.author: HaMMeReD
comments.body:
GTA6 will probably be the single largest piece of media ever created by humanity without the use of generative AI (or at least, probably only on some of the code to a limited extent).

GTA7 unlikely can't just do the same (up the budget and scale) and compete in 10-15 years. That doesn't mean that it can't exist, but it's not going to be a continuation of the tech ladder as it is now. 

I guess if I was to project out a 10 year timeframe, that's like EOL PS6 early life PS7 maybe. So we are 1.5->2 generations ahead. We'll have a lot more inference so things like DLSS and Path tracing will be the norm. Animations, Physics, Material responses are all going to be AI backed by that point. We'll probably see good soft body physics, fluid simulations things like that.

Realtime generative might be an opportunity on that horizon as well. Where the game just renders wireframes and context clues and the renderer does a custom generative pass, bringing whatever aesthetic to the table. Line art, comic, realistic, anime, etc. So it's possible it splits to world building and aesthetic building, and generative bridges the two teams.

It's really hard to say, we haven't seen any massive AI productions yet, but at some point the floodgates will open, so it's hard to say what the 10yr horizon for games is. It'd be a bit of risky time to start, but if you are R\* big, you can influence industry to make a game over that horizon.
